We ordered that our equipment and weaponry be inventorised and upgraded in order for us to be well prepared in the event of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you want to add anything else?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: That were many other things that needed to be attended to, but the important thing is to say that measures were developed in order to ensure permanent, active and passive duty service at the work-place and duty on call of all the various organisational units in order to ensure efficiency of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When a state of war was declared on the 24th of March, 1999, how did the public security sector operate from then on?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, when a state of war was declared, the Ministry of the Interior had its regular tasks to perform but under different circumstances with far more staff and increased duties. We performed regular public security duties during the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how work was organised at the MUP headquarters during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: As far as the seat of the ministry is concerned, we had problems because many organisational units were detached. And that's why the minister, together with the sector chief, toured these locations, and I went to see them as well together with the fire prevention police chief, Mr. Slobodan Spasic, and several other attendant services. We relocated other services as well, such as the crime police; the finance service was also relocated. There were many others; I don't want to enumerate them all here. We had round-the-clock duty stints which were performed at a place we called "the staff." There were assistant ministers and others who took turns, and there was also the fire prevention police representative there. Every night we had the general area bombed; there were fires, and our forces, including fire brigades, had to be organised in order to address all these problems in a timely fashion. We also had to draw up reports and send them to the minister in a timely fashion, and then the minister would inform the government and other state agencies accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the collegium of the minister meet during the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it did. Although, of course, the circumstances were far more difficult. We held collegium meetings at different locations, and these meetings were attended by the minister, together with assistants for the departments of public and state security and chiefs of administrations of public security. So more or less the same people who had attended these meetings before continued doing so during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In 1999, during the war, therefore, who was at the head of the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic. He was the chief of the public security sector during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who planned, organised, and directed anti- terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija in 1999, i.e., during the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: During the war in 1999, it was the staff of the Ministry of the Interior for the prevention of terrorism that planned, organised, and directed anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the collegium meetings of the public security sector, did you consider reports received from the staff for anti-terrorist activities, and did you consider tasks related to the implementation of anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: Not once during the war did we discuss planning, organising, and implementation of anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija. On the other hand, we also did not consider any reports which had to do with the prevention of terrorism. I repeat that we had logistics requirements. It was the police administration and the administration for shared affairs that reported to the minister on their activities and appropriate decisions were taken. The police administration reported to the minister on the needs of the units and their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war did you co-operate with Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, chief of the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: Yes, we cooperated since we were housed in the same building or the same locations as the minister, and we cooperated closely. At times it would be him, at times it would be me who would be sent by the minister to the pogroms, that is, to the towns that had suffered great destruction around Belgrade, so we would see each other every day, work together, prepared various decrees that had to be sent to the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what were your activities during the war in 1999 as assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: As assistant minister in charge of fire-fighting police forces and communications, actually encountered a lot of problems. I was up all night, practically every night, together with General Slobodan Spasic, in order to organise our forces, in order to deal with the major consequences of bombing, to save human lives, and so on and so forth. If that sense, I was in constant touch with the relevant ministries pursuant to the instruction of the minister in order to secure the required technical equipment and means in order to be able to carry out our assignments successfully. And then as far as communications are concerned, since I'm not a communications expert, I also had considerable problems in order to organise the communications in the best possible way. We had considerable problems because the secretariat building in Kosovo was destroyed which was our special centre. The ministry in Belgrade also had the systems room destroyed, which is where the equipment such as the special telephone exchange and the telegraph networks were housed. I don't want to go into too many details, but there was a lot of work. And, of course, we were all so busy in the field in the basic organisational units issuing instructions to them about what they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's time for the break now, so please tell me just how the shifts were organised at the MUP staff or the headquarters? How were they organised in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: The shifts in the MUP were organised. Every night, a number of people were on active duty and some were on passive duty. There were lists. There were some people who were on duty, including the chief of the public security sector. He was also on duty. It was our job to not only organise the work on the clearing up of the consequences, but also to urgently inform the state leadership, the prime minister, and the president of the Republic of Serbia about the situation and the consequences and about the measures that were being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have kept half of my promise, and we can go for the break now. But I do still have a little bit left, a little bit of time I need to complete my cross-examination [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. We will have the second break now. We expect to be able to resume just after 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we look at D440.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your binder, this is in tab 13, General. This is a dispatch from the public security station dated the 27th of March, 1999, signed by the assistant to the minister, Major-General Stojan Misic. Can you please tell us during the war exactly what your activities were altogether?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: Amongst other things, I as assistant minister was tasked with taking measures from the areas that I was covering to issue the relevant instructions and directions to the Secretariats of Internal Affairs in the field in order to implement certain decisions or regulations that had to do with the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you explain to whom this dispatch was sent?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: This dispatch was sent to the Federal Ministry of Internal Affairs for information purposes because this is the execution of a decision by a federal organ. It was also sent to all the Secretariats of Internal Affairs, border control stations, the MUP HQ in Pristina, and, for purposes of information, to the relevant organisational units at the seat of the ministry, or rather, the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us what does this dispatch deal with, what kind of problem?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: Instructions are issued here to update the lists of foreigners with permanent residence and foreigners with temporary residence and also make all other preparations for the issuance of travel documents to military conscripts and in that sense the secretariats are instructed as to the measures they need to take in order to carry out this dispatch. Let me just repeat: All the things that the minister tasked me with from my area of work we would, in turn, instruct the parties in the field as to how they should execute certain tasks pursuant to the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 1D9 now. D259, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is in tab 14, General, in your binder. And we are looking at a dispatch from the public security station of the 9th of April, 1999, which is signed by assistant minister Major-General Stojan Misic. I would like to ask you to whom this dispatch was sent?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: It was sent to all the Secretariats of Internal Affairs, also to the border police stations and the MUP staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please tell us what is the subject of this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: The subject of this dispatch are the relevant decrees because the federal government adopted the Decree on the restrictions on foreign travel by military conscripts of the Yugoslav Army and the Decree on time limits in court, administrative and misdemeanor procedures during the state of war. And it also issued a decree implementing the Law on the Transport of Hazardous Materials during the state of war. The Government of the Republic of Serbia also proposed that relevant decrees be adopted by the president of the Republic of Serbia, including the decree on the assembly of citizens during the state of war during -- on the residence of citizens during the war and the issuance of ID cards. I sent this instruction in order for the regulations adopted by the federal government and the decree issued by the president of the Republic of Serbia to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D261 now, on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is in tab 15 in your binder, sir. This is a dispatch by the public security department of the 19th of April, 1999, signed by assistant minister Major-General Stojan Misic. Can you please tell us to whom this dispatch was sent?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: The dispatch was sent on the 19th of April, 1999, to all the Secretariats for Internal Affairs in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is the subject of this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: Its subject are administrative tasks, and I said before that I was in charge of that area, amongst other things, and in view of the fact that with the beginning of the NATO forces aggression on our country, certain problems were caused regarding the residence of citizens and the issue of personal ID cards. In the state of war, the manner of working in these administrative assignments was being changed. We also said that as far as the Law on Social Organisations and Citizens Associations was concerned, adequate measures needed to be taken pursuant to the way in which we formulated that in our dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at Exhibit D447 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And this is tab 16 in your binder, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page please in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch of the RJB of the 19th of -- of the 30th of April, 1999, signed by assistant minister Major-General Stojan Misic. General, can you please tell us to whom the dispatch was sent?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: The dispatch was also sent to all the Secretariats of Internal Affairs, the border police stations, the MUP staff in Pristina. It was sent to the three administrations at the seat, the operations centre also at the seat of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is the subject of this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: We are here informing about how the General Staff and their information centre established a new protocol for the war-time press card, and we instruct that in future journalists cannot work without a new working press card and permission to work accompanying the issuance of that card.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at D254.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is in tab 17 in your binder, sir. This is RJB dispatch of the 4th of May, 1999, signed by assistant minister chief of the RJB, Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic. Can you please tell us to whom this dispatch was sent?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: The dispatch was sent to the Secretariats of Internal Affairs, the MUP staff in Pristina, the border control stations, the police administrations, the criminal police administration, traffic police administration, border police administration, fire-fighting police administration, and the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us what the topic of this dispatch is? 17 A. This dispatch deals with the experiences of the members of the Ministry in numerous interventions in fire-fighting, redirecting transport, clearing up of debris, and so on and so forth. In view of the experiences we acquired in the process of this type of work, we said that in the future additional measures needed to be taken in order to achieve even better results. And in that sense we were instructing the secretariats about what they would need to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us if you took part in the work on this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Together with my associate, I took part in the drafting of this dispatch. Other administrations also participated because these are several professional lines of work and what each professional line needed to do in order to complete its job successfully. A number of professional lines of work were covered, and that is why the chief of the public security department, General Vlastimir Djordjevic, signed this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, we've looked at a number of dispatches of this type, can you please tell me if the minister of Internal Affairs was familiar with the contents of this type of dispatch, and if so, in what way?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC
utterances.text: Since these are dispatches covering - if we are talking about these particular ones - several lines of professional duties, and in view of the seriousness as far as the direction of the services in its execution of specific assignments, the dispatch would then be given either to the assistant minister or several professional lines of work covered, to the chief of the department. In that way, they would then need to go to the minister so that the minister would agree that such a dispatch would be sent out. These are dispatches of a more serious nature, conditionally speaking, compared to those signed by administrations discussing certain specific topics. This is the establishment of organisational and functional preconditions, and that is why the top leadership of the ministry would need to sign that with the prior permission of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General, for testifying. Your Honours, thank you very much. I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz, we've heard that the witness has had surgery in recent times. That causes us to ask whether you think you can be confident to complete cross-examination, if it commenced tomorrow, in the course of tomorrow's session?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I commence tomorrow, I'm almost certain I'll complete tomorrow. I'll stick to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that would allow a little time for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That should, Your Honour. I don't want to commit myself to too much, but that should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we keep pushing you, you see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you heard the thrust of that. If we would sit if it was necessary to finish the evidence of the witness by tomorrow evening, but it seems probable that we can conclude the evidence tomorrow even though we adjourn now, and that would be in the interests, we assess, of the witness, to minimise the strain on him. That being so, we would propose to adjourn now, even though it's just over half an hour early, to continue tomorrow at 2.15 with a view to concluding the evidence of the witness in the course of tomorrow afternoon's session. You have followed that, I suspect, General. We will adjourn early tonight rather than start a completely different aspect of your evidence which is cross-examination. We propose to continue tomorrow at 2.15. Counsel indicate that we should expect to finish your evidence tomorrow. So we will take that course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will adjourn now until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of April, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
